name: 19-Nor-4-androstenedione (19-norandrostenedione)

lead: 19-Norandrostenedione is a prohormone that converts to nandrolone in the body. Bodybuilders used it in the US supplement era, until 2005, for more muscle mass.

After oral intake it converts to nandrolone and shares its urinary metabolite. The research on it centres on doping tests rather than muscle outcomes; a 2000 JAMA study looked at trace contamination of androstenedione products and whether ingestion causes positive tests for a nandrolone metabolite.

paras: It was taken orally as an over-the-counter supplement and stacked in bodybuilding routines. It is no longer legally sold in the US.
It is US Schedule III and prohibited in sport. Contaminated supplements have caused positive nandrolone tests.

angle.text: This prohormone converts to nandrolone, which activates androgen receptors and supports muscle growth. It was sold over the counter in the US until 2005 and used by bodybuilders; published work on it focuses on doping tests, not physique outcomes.

lead: 19-Nor-4-androstenedione, also called 19-norandrostenedione or bolandione, is a steroid that is a precursor of nandrolone. It was sold over the counter in the US as a prohormone supplement until 2005.[1]

It is best documented in the literature through doping research. A 2000 JAMA study found trace contamination of over-the-counter androstenedione products and examined whether androstenedione and 19-norandrostenedione ingestion causes positive urine tests for a nandrolone metabolite.[2]

paras: Wikipedia reports that it converts readily to nandrolone orally and binds the androgen receptor about ten times less potently than DHT.[1] It is also a 19-nor steroid like those found naturally in small quantities, for example in human ovarian follicular fluid, where 19-norandrostenedione and 19-nortestosterone have been measured.[3]

Because it and nandrolone share the urinary metabolite 19-norandrosterone, contaminated supplements can yield positive tests.[2][1] A registered phase 1/2 trial (started 2006, 20 participants) studied the risk of positive doping tests after ingesting supplements contaminated with trace nandrolone metabolites.[4]

The 2000 JAMA study assessed the purity of over-the-counter androstenedione and whether administration of androstenedione or 19-norandrostenedione leads to positive tests for a nandrolone metabolite.[2] A completed trial, NCT00682123, evaluated positive-test risk from contaminated supplements.[4] No trials have evaluated muscle or appearance outcomes.

timeline.event: JAMA study on trace contamination and nandrolone-metabolite positives.[2]
